summary: Describes a protocol that supports 3270 terminal devices more fully than traditional tn3270 practice does, such as device naming and printer support. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: TN3270E adds device selection, printer support, optional functions, and response handling to 3270 sessions carried over Telnet. Client and server negotiate what they both support before sending 3270 data.

questions: how does tn3270e negotiate a device name
what is the tn3270e message header
subtitle: A Telnet option for negotiating 3270 terminals, printers, device names, functions, and message responses.

tldr.problem: Traditional tn3270 did not provide standard printer emulation, device-name requests, consistent special-key support, or SNA response handling.
tldr.mechanism: TN3270E negotiates a device type and optional name, then a supported function list. Each data message carries a five-byte header describing its type and response information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2355 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1647 and is updated by RFC 6270. A client or server may decline TN3270E and use traditional tn3270.

today: RFC 2355 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1647 and is updated by RFC 6270.

sections.title: Limits of Traditional tn3270
sections.content:
Traditional tn3270 commonly negotiated Terminal-Type, Binary Transmission, and End of Record before exchanging the 3270 data stream. RFC 2355 lists gaps in that practice: printer emulation, device-name selection, ATTN and SYSREQ support, SNA responses, and access to Bind information.

TN3270E is a Telnet option that defines how these capabilities are negotiated. If either peer declines it, the connection can use traditional tn3270.
sections.plainLanguage: Traditional tn3270 did not provide a standard way to choose printers or device names and lacked several functions. TN3270E adds negotiation for these features.

sections.title: The Negotiation Sequence
sections.content:
The TN3270E Telnet option has code 40. Agreement also implies binary transmission and end-of-record support in both directions. The default is not to use TN3270E.

After agreeing to the option, the peers negotiate device type and possibly a device name. They negotiate functions only after the device request succeeds, and exchange 3270 data only after both negotiations complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Client and server first agree to TN3270E. They then select a device and functions before sending 3270 data.

sections.title: Choosing a Device and Name
sections.content:
The client requests a terminal or printer type. It may use CONNECT to request a specific device or a named pool, or use ASSOCIATE to request a printer paired with a terminal it previously received. A request cannot use both commands.

The server accepts the complete request and returns the assigned device name, or rejects it with a reason code. Device and resource names should not exceed 8 bytes. Terminal types include IBM-3278 models and IBM-DYNAMIC; the printer type is IBM-3287-1.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can request a device type, a specific name, a named pool, or a printer paired with a terminal. The server either accepts the request and returns a device name or rejects it with a reason.

sections.title: Agreeing on Session Functions
sections.content:
After device negotiation, the client proposes a function list. The other peer accepts the exact list or returns a different list to reject the proposal and continue negotiation. A peer must not re-add a function that the other side already removed.

The functions cover printer control codes, 3270 printer data, positive and negative responses, SNA Bind information, and SYSREQ. A printer session must agree on SCS-CTL-CODES, DATA-STREAM-CTL, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side proposes the optional functions it supports. They can exchange revised lists until they agree or end TN3270E negotiation.

sections.title: The Five-Byte Data Header
sections.content:
Every TN3270E data message has a five-byte header, data if present, and a Telnet IAC EOR marker. The header contains DATA-TYPE, REQUEST-FLAG, RESPONSE-FLAG, and a two-byte SEQ-NUMBER.

DATA-TYPE tells the receiver how to interpret the data. With the RESPONSES function, sequence numbers correlate responses to messages and count from zero through 32767. A data byte of decimal 255 is doubled so Telnet does not treat it as a command.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the message data and, when negotiated, whether a response is expected. A sequence number lets the peers match a response to the message it concerns.

sections.title: Modes, Responses and Special Keys
sections.content:
A session begins in 3270 mode and can switch to NVT mode by sending the other data type. With RESPONSES, the receiver can report success or an error. The server can send PRINT-EOJ at the end of a printer job.

ATTN is carried using Telnet Interrupt Process and can be translated by an SNA server. SYSREQ uses Telnet Abort Output to suspend normal data flow; the user can return to the session by sending it again.
sections.plainLanguage: TN3270E can switch between 3270 and NVT data and can report processing results. It maps ATTN and SYSREQ to Telnet commands with defined server behavior.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TN3270E adds no security protection beyond ordinary Telnet. The RFC says a session is no more secure than a normal Telnet session.

Authentication mechanisms defined for Telnet could also be used to decide whether a user may use a particular terminal or printer name.
sections.plainLanguage: TN3270E does not add authentication or privacy protection. Any security depends on the Telnet mechanisms used by the connection.

fields.name: DATA-TYPE
fields.desc: Identifies how the message data is interpreted.

fields.name: RESPONSE-FLAG
fields.desc: States whether a response is expected or gives its result.

fields.name: SEQ-NUMBER
fields.desc: Matches responses to data messages when RESPONSES is negotiated.
